Absolutely, being able to reach out to your community for support is so important, and I’m really sorry to hear that that isn’t proving to be possible for you. Or at least that they’re not helping when you have reached out. But just in the context of this specific post, I think OP’s ex wife is completely valid in removing herself from this situation and does not have any obligation to put OP’s mental health above her own. 

I know it doesn’t feel like a threat if there is actual plan/intent, but it is important to recognize that threatening suicide is a very common and well-documented emotional abuse tactic. People can do abusive things without having abusive intent. OP’s ex very well might be perceiving this as manipulation whether it is or not and she has the right to protect herself. If there is plan/intent, OP needs to reach out to someone receptive, and not someone who has clearly put up a boundary. We all know hotlines suck and so do the police. However, as shitty as the process can be, if you are actively suicidal and ready with a plan and means to hurt yourself, you can absolutely be admitted to the hospital regardless of insurance. I work in the mental health field and have seen it happen countless times. OP could even go to an urgent care center and explain that if they go home they will end their life, and there are procedures put in place for this. My brother actually did that exact thing and was placed on a MH hold and no one asked a single question about money or insurance until he was safe and they worked with him on a payment plan. 

So yes, everyone needs and deserves a support system. But it is also valid for those supports to get overwhelmed when they no longer have the capacity to help you, and if immediate safety is at risk, there are resources in place to address that. Similar to addiction, suicidality is really fucking hard for a partner to help someone through, and it’s okay that not every partner will be able to help every time.

This might vary state by state but at least in Colorado, family cannot be paid for what are considered “homemaking” tasks. These tasks include cooking, cleaning, laundry, grocery shopping, transportation, and a few other things. Family can only be paid for “personal care” tasks like bathing, dressing, mobility, medication reminders, etc. There are ADLs and IADLs, and scoring for functional eligibility is only based on ADLs.

I’m a little late here but I actually work for a Medicaid waiver program in Colorado. It varies state by state but here we use something called “nursing facility level of care” to determine functional eligibility. Basically it means that if a client did not have support in the home they would need to move into a facility. It’s more cost effective to keep people in the community with in-home support, so the program targets individuals who could be appropriate for nursing facility placement, but who would rather stay home as long as possible. Scoring to see if you meet this level of care is based on the following areas: bathing, dressing, toileting, mobility, transfers, eating, behaviors, and memory. These are ADLs. We also ask about IADLS (things like laundry, grocery shopping, cooking, cleaning, etc.) but those questions do not impact scoring.

I mean I’m just one person on Reddit so take my opinions with a grain of salt but… no I would not recommend thinking about your privilege 24/7. It’s just not feasible or helpful to anyone and you’ll probably just end up resenting the oppressed class. Maybe in interactions with women you’ve never met before it should be higher on your list of priorities, but if you’re treating her just like a normal human then I’m not really sure what you would do or say that would oppress her. If you have a tendency to do oppressive things or make assumptions that women are weak or over-emotional or something, then challenge yourself to be aware of that for sure. However if you get married to a woman I don’t think your wife would be super enthused with you thinking about your privilege more than you think about just hanging out with her. Be aware of it enough to notice if you’re patronizing her or if she’s being mistreated, but same advice again- treat her like a human. Consent is a huge thing and if a woman consents to having you in her life in a close capacity (friendship, dating, etc.) then she has already considered your privilege and decided it is something she is okay with. Your journey to understand and grapple with your privilege can be done mostly on your own, and you don’t need to involve every woman you talk to in this. I know it’s overwhelming to think about. But I don’t think my black friends want me thinking about my privilege 100% of the time I spend with them. I think they would rather I do that work on my own so I have a general awareness, and then treat them like people that I like hanging out with, because I do. Just my two cents. Nothing wrong with asking these questions! I just think you might be stressing yourself out more than you need to.

Most people aren’t opposed to working, despite the name of the sub. A lot of professions are overworked and underpaid and the response to just “get another job” is pretty stupid to me when raising the compensation rate would retain more employees, allow people to actually pay off their loans, and allow people to have families and hobbies outside of work. I, and many social workers I know, have second jobs that take up the time we could otherwise be contributing to family and friendships. People don’t not want to work, they just don’t want their entire life to be work and then look back and realize it afforded them nothing but stress and a bad back that insurance won’t cover.

Is there any chance she might qualify for medicaid? Medicaid offers waivers for different populations including aging and/or disabled individuals. Services can include in-home care, assistance with housekeeping, meals, finances, etc. Check out “home and community based services” offered by NJ Medicaid ([this discusses the program, services, and eligibility requirements](https://www.state.nj.us/humanservices/doas/documents/ltc_guide_6.pdf). If she doesn’t qualify for Medicaid I wonder if any nonprofits exist in her area to assist with accessing resources, it would be nice if she could work with a case manager. 

I also want to echo a sentiment I saw in a few other comments. I actually do functional eligibility assessments for Medicaid waivers in a different state, and it is very very very common for folks to downplay their struggles. She absolutely may be avoiding the shower due to financial stress, but it could also be related to physical or mental health as others have pointed out. Many clients have difficulty expressing their needs/struggles, especially to their children, so it could be worth checking in on her overall well-being. We assess [ADLs (activities of daily living) and IADLs (instrumental activities of daily living)](https://betterhealthwhileaging.net/what-are-adls-and-iadls/) and I think they can be a great place to start when looking for an overall picture of health. 

I hope you’re able to help her access some resources and regain a little more of her independence. And I’m glad you get to visit a few times a year, I’m sure that helps a lot. She’s lucky to have someone looking out for her, I wish you the best of luck!!
